question: Why do nurses take baseline neurological data when a patient is first admitted?

options.A: To compare with later findings to detect clinical changes
options.B: To calculate the patient's exact hospital discharge date
options.C: To determine the exact cause of a brain tumor
options.D: To replace the need for physician daily rounds

explanation: Having a clear starting point helps you quickly spot any tiny changes if the patient's condition starts to slip later! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why do nurses keep doing frequent neuro checks for unstable patients?

options.A: To catch early signs of rising intracranial pressure
options.B: To ensure the patient stays awake all night long
options.C: To keep the patient's family members from worrying
options.D: To prevent the patient from asking too many questions

explanation: Things can change fast in acute care. Frequent checks help you catch warning signs of pressure in the brain early, way before serious damage happens. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which health history complaint needs an urgent neurological check right away?

options.A: Occasional muscle cramps after heavy exercise
options.B: Sudden changes in speech and vision
options.C: Temporary skin dryness in cold weather
options.D: Mild fatigue after a full night of sleep

explanation: Sudden trouble talking or seeing are major warning signs for a stroke or another urgent brain emergency. Always stay alert for these! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h2)

question: Why is it important to ask a patient about their current medications during a neuro history?

options.A: Medications completely cure all neurological disorders
options.B: Many drugs can alter mental status or cause tremors
options.D: Drugs are the only cause of sudden vision loss

explanation: Certain drugs and everyday meds can make a patient feel confused or cause shaky hands, which can easily look like a brain problem if you don't check their drug history. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h2)

question: How does a lethargic patient usually act during an assessment?

options.A: Completely unresponsive even to painful stimuli
options.B: Fully awake and answers every question instantly
options.C: Aggressive and physically combative with staff
options.D: Drowsy and drifts off to sleep when not stimulated

explanation: A lethargic patient wakes up when you talk to them or touch them, but they tend to drift right back off to sleep the moment you stop interacting. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h3)

question: A patient only opens their eyes and groans when you firmly pinch their shoulder. How do you document this level of consciousness?
explanation: A stuporous patient is deeply sleepy and only reacts with sounds or movement when given strong or painful stimulation. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h3)

question: Which cranial nerve controls the muscles for chewing and lets you feel sensations on your face?
explanation: Cranial Nerve V (the trigeminal nerve) is responsible for feeling things on your face and helping you chew your food. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h4)

question: How do you properly test Cranial Nerve VII (the Facial nerve)?

options.A: By asking the patient to identify different sweet and salty tastes
options.B: By observing facial symmetry while the patient smiles and frowns
options.C: By checking if the tongue stays straight when sticking it out
options.D: By testing the corneal blink reflex using a cotton wisp

explanation: Since CN VII controls facial expressions, watching if both sides of the face move evenly when they smile or frown is the best test! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h4)

question: What is the highest possible score on a standard muscle strength testing scale?
explanation: Muscle power is graded from 0 to 5. A score of 5 means the patient has normal strength and can push hard against your full resistance. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h5)

question: You ask a patient to touch their own nose and then touch your finger over and over. What are you testing?
explanation: The finger-to-nose test checks the cerebellum, which is the part of the brain that keeps your body movements smooth and coordinated. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h5)

question: What does 'stereognosis' mean during a sensory exam?

options.A: Recognizing a number traced on the skin of the palm
options.B: Sensing the vibration of a tuning fork on a bony joint
options.C: Identifying a familiar object placed in the hand by touch
options.D: Telling the difference between sharp and dull pinpricks

explanation: Stereognosis is the brain's cool ability to recognize everyday items like a key or coin just by feeling them in the hand with eyes closed. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h6)

question: Why should you ask a patient to close their eyes during a sensory touch test?

options.A: To measure if the patient can stay awake under stress
options.B: To prevent visual cues from helping them guess the stimulus
options.C: To help the patient fall asleep during a long examination
options.D: To protect the eyes from bright room lights and glare

explanation: Closing their eyes ensures they rely purely on their nerves and touch, rather than cheating by peeking at what you are doing! [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h6)

question: What score shows a normal, healthy deep tendon reflex?
explanation: A score of 2+ is the standard, expected normal response for deep tendon reflexes in healthy adults. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h7)

question: What does a 4+ reflex score with jerky muscle spasms (clonus) usually point to?
explanation: Extremely brisk reflexes with clonus mean there is likely an issue or irritation in the central nervous system (brain or spinal cord). [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h7)

question: Which test is mainly used to check electrical brain waves and diagnose seizures?
explanation: An EEG places tiny sensors on the scalp to record brain electrical activity, making it the go-to test for seizure disorders. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h8)

question: What is the main benefit of getting a CT scan or MRI for a neurological patient?

options.A: Measuring electrical wave patterns during sleep cycles
options.B: Providing detailed structural images of the brain tissue
options.C: Checking cranial nerve function in unconscious patients
options.D: Testing superficial and deep tendon reflex strength

explanation: CT and MRI scans let doctors see cross-section pictures of what is happening inside the skull, like bleeding, swelling, or tumors. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h8)

question: Why is it important to write clear behavioral details in your notes instead of vague words?

options.A: To guarantee that the patient is discharged without home care
options.B: To provide clear, objective data for other healthcare team members
options.C: To replace the need for verbal shift-to-shift report handoffs
options.D: To reduce the total number of nursing shifts required in a week

explanation: Writing exact details prevents guesswork and helps every nurse on the team track whether the patient is getting better or worse. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h9)

question: What is the biggest risk of waiting too long to report a sudden drop in a patient's neuro status?

options.A: It increases the financial cost of hospital room supplies
options.B: It causes the nursing documentation to look untidy
options.C: It can delay life-saving interventions for acute brain injury
options.D: It forces the patient to stay in the hospital an extra day

explanation: Brain emergencies move fast! Reporting changes immediately can be the difference between a full recovery and permanent damage. [learn more](GNS222_U3_T2#GNS222_U3_T2_h9)
